utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy being absent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy being absent, we sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Milosevic, to complete your examination-in-chief. And remember, we're working for the end of the first session for the completion, concentrating on the substance of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. Robinson, that I am always focused on the substance, and I will try to finish before the end of the first session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, towards the end of the last session, we covered events in Bistrazin, Djakovica, events involving the column that had been bombed, and we discussed certain issues involving the victims. In addition to that column you spoke about yesterday, the column of refugees on the road between Djakovica and Prizren and later in the Djakovica hospital, so in addition to that column, the bombs also hit another column of Albanian refugees that was on its way back to its homes in the village, a column that had stopped to rest. Do you know about them?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this case. It happened in the night of the 13th of May, 1999, on the road between Prizren and Suva Reka, five kilometres away from Prizren, in a place called Korisa. About 600 internally displaced Albanians had stopped to rest. They were hit by thermovisual bombs that develop an extremely high temperature. Eighty people died on the spot, including 30 children, including some infants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us see a videotape depicting the bombing of the refugees in Korisa village, 14 May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, this was a column that had stopped for a while. Just a minute. On the screen we see members of the staff. This is part of the next video clip. Will you please wait with this video clip. We will play it later. Here where you see the people who were hit with these bombs, we see scattered bodies and destroyed tractors, that was a column of Albanian refugees that had stopped for a while to rest, as you said. There were no buses there. There were no cars. It was perfectly obvious that there were only tractors, vehicles used solely by villagers.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, with this evidence. First of all, the defendant -- the accused is leading material. Secondly, where is it relevant in any event? That's a matter we've canvassed before. Third, has the accused stopped to consider that the evidence that's already been put in by the Prosecution about this material is adequate and sufficient? Because none of this is probably in dispute so far as the Prosecution is concerned who have led evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Nice, it may very well be relevant. I'm about to ask the witness what he can tell us about the refugees. Why were they fleeing? Where were they fleeing from? That's very relevant to the indictment, because your allegations are that refugees fled because of crimes committed by the Serbs. The accused's case is that there was another reason for the refugees fleeing. So that is the -- that's how this matter becomes relevant, in my view, and those are the questions that Mr. Milosevic should now be putting to the witness, if he has the information. Professor, can you tell us anything more about these -- this column of 600 refugees? Do you know where they were coming from and in what circumstances they left their homes, whether they left -- what caused them to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a column from the region of Suva Reka, for the most part, and they had set out after the NATO aggression began. They left their homes on the way to Albania. However, halfway there, they decided to turn back. From Prizren, returning to Suva Reka, they stopped in Korisa village where they decided to stay the night, and the next day they were supposed to continue their way back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say they left after the NATO aggression began? That needs clarification. It's an issue in the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the beginning of the NATO aggression, the population of Kosovo and Metohija, regardless of ethnicity, started leaving Kosovo en masse. That means Albanians, Serbs, everybody who was living there started to leave, started to flee. That was why people sought refuge elsewhere where they would be able to live peacefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have any specific information about this particular column, as to why they left, or is this just a generalisation on your part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from what I said, I have no additional information, at least in relation to this column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the question raised by Judge Robinson and in view of what you said about the fact that they had stopped to rest, then it must have been known for several hours, at least, that it was a column that was returning to its village. Their destination, their intention must have been known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can't put a question in that way, that's leading, that it must have been known that they were returning to their village. That's a leading question, and that is what Mr. Nice complains of all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not suggest to him in the form of a leading question that they were going back to their own village. He said himself that they had stopped to rest, so he knew they were returning back home. I'm just asking him if there were any comments made as to NATO choosing to bomb precisely columns of refugees returning to their homes. Yesterday, we called -- we talked about columns from Bistrazin and Djakovica, and this one is from Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the time that you remember in relation to this event, were there any comments heard made about columns returning homes -- returning home being bombed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because this was not the only one. Several columns had been bombed. The territory of Kosovo and Metohija was to be completely emptied of Albanians. However, since there were many internally displaced Albanians who were returning home, that did not fit with the scenario. We had already managed to convince several thousands to stay put and remain at home or return home, and that was the official policy of the state authorities of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andric. Please look at tab 5.11. You will find there several photographs that are also available on CD. Maybe we can see them on the monitors, on the computer if the AV booth is ready. If not, then I will ask for at least a couple of these photographs to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are photographs of the scenes that we saw in the video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 5.10 to be an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is 5.11 now. I'm looking at these photos. You said that the bombs used were a kind of bombs that develop a high temperature.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so-called thermovision bombs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take one of these photos and tell us what this is all about, the fifth or the sixth photograph.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see charred bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just put a couple of photos on the ELMO. That will suffice.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the tractor-trailer, again we see charged bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document under 5.11 be also tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, Mr. Andric, Mr. Robinson replied to an observation made by Mr. Nice and said or, rather, asked were people fleeing from the bombs or were they fleeing before our policemen and army. But before I ask my question, I will read to you only a couple of quotations from this Kosovo indictment. I hope I don't need to provide you with a copy, because my quoting will be very brief. But just before I do that, one question. You lived in Pristina at the time; is that correct? And you just mentioned Prizren, Djakovica So you had moved around that territory, including Prizren and Djakovica, and you probably visited some other places that I don't have time to mention. I will read to you from paragraph 63. It is a rather long paragraph in the indictment, but for instance, 63(B) says -- it refers to Prizren, and I will later ask you if you know anything about this and if there is any truth in this. In the B/C/S version, it's page 17. 63(b) Prizren: "On 25 March 1999 the village of Pirane was surrounded by forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia, tanks and various military vehicles. The village was shelled and a number of the residents were killed."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the accused be asked to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, and I will also skip certain sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Thereafter, forces of the FRY and Serbia entered the village and burned the houses of Kosovo Albanians. ... Some of the Kosovo Albanians fleeing towards Srbica were killed or wounded by snipers. Forces of the FRY and Serbia then launched an offensive in the area of Srbica and shelled the villages of Donji Retimlje, Retimle, and Randubrava. Kosovo Albanian villagers were forced from their homes and sent to the Albanian border." Now, pay attention to this date. It says: "From 28 March 1999, in the city of Prizren, forces of the FRY and Serbia went from house to house, ordering Kosovo Albanian residents to leave. They were forced to join convoys of vehicles and persons travelling on foot to the Albanian border. En route, members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia beat and killed Kosovo Albanian men, separated Kosovo Albanian women from the convoy and sexually assaulted the women. At the border, all personal documents were taken away by forces of the FRY and Serbia." Now, I have read out this paragraph to you. Tell me what you know about it. You have been to Prizren. You have been to Djakovica. You were there at the relevant time. Tell us, what do you know about all this?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period from the 1st of April, 1999, up until the 15th of April, I was very often visiting that area. With my teams, I followed, escorted precisely those columns leaving towards Albania, towards Vrbnica. I claim with full responsibility that not in a single day did I see any members of either the Ministry of Interior or the army of Yugoslavia who made the slightest move towards making an illicit, unlawful act. On the contrary, the MUP and the army were trying to help us and the refugees. As for sexual assaults, I believe I need not waste my breath even to comment upon this. As for attacks on columns, I spent four or five days near the border. I didn't see it with my own eyes, but I heard about such cases. I believe that it indeed happened that personal documents were taken away. I don't think it was done following some orders. It was done as a precaution maybe, because these documents could have been abused. There Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is a central computer at the level of the state of Serbia where all the citizens of Serbia are registered. So any citizen of Serbia, even if they lost their IDs, could get new IDs. The fact that somebody lost an ID doesn't mean that one is erased from the records as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but it says here they were driven out of their homes and sent to the Albanian border. Did anybody drive Albanians out of their homes and send them to the border?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the people in the columns. There were women, children, and elderly people. I spoke to many of them. Nobody told me any such thing. Everybody told me, on the contrary, that they were running away from NATO bombs and they were looking to find a peaceful area where they would be safe from the bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to skip a few things, although I'm sorry, but I have some more quotations. Let us look at paragraph 63(G). It says: "Pristina." Starting with 24th March, 1999, and continuing through the end of May 1999, did you live in Pristina at the time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were there all the time except you were making tours of other places. So it goes on to say: "... Serbian police went to the homes of Kosovo Albanians in the city of Pristina and forced the residents to leave. During the course of these forced expulsions, a number of people were killed. Many of those forced from their homes went directly to the train station, while others sought shelter in nearby neighbourhoods. Hundreds of ethnic Albanians, guided by Serb police at all the intersections, gathered at the train station and then were loaded onto overcrowded trains or buses after a long wait during which time," et cetera, et cetera. "Those on the trains went as far as Djeneral Jankovic, a village near the Macedonian border. During the train ride, many people had their identification papers taken from them. After getting off the trains, forces of the FRY and Serbia told the Kosovo Albanians to walk along the tracks into Macedonia since the surrounding land had been mined. Those who tried to hide in Pristina were eventually expelled in a similar fashion. During the course of these forced expulsions, a number of these -- a number of these people were killed and several women were sexually assaulted." And again in (G) we find that Serb forces entered villages around Pristina, looted their property, robbed them of their money, et cetera. What do you know about this, Dr. Andric?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this time I was in Pristina. From time to time I was out in the field, but I would spend several hours a day in Pristina. I know about all this only from television, and I assert with full responsibility that it was not the Serbian police that did this. I do not dispute that there were individual instances of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "this"?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people forcing someone to leave their home. But these were not policemen. These were criminals. It was wartime, and these criminals perhaps thought they were helping their country and their people by this. This is absolutely untrue. However, all of these have been tried and some have even been convicted. The police never did this. The police protected those people. It's true that they directed them in the direction they wanted to go. They tried to persuade them to return, but they couldn't prevent them from leaving the territory of Kosovo and Metohija if they were intent on fleeing and searching for safety for their families and shelter from the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at Djakovica. You were in Djakovica. Under (h): "Those who were walking on foot were directed to several border crossings, and those who were on vehicles were directed towards the town of Prizren." And then it says: "Starting on the 24th of March or thereabouts until the 11th of May, the forces of the FRY and Serbia started forcing the inhabitants of the town of Djakovica to leave." Do you have any information about the forces of FRY and Serbia forcing an Albanian to leave his home?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a single piece of information about this. I was out on the ground for several days. I accompanied the convoy leaving Kosovo and Metohija. It consisted mostly of farmers from that area. We gave them assistance in every possible way, and not from a single Albanian did I hear anything like this. I have no reason not to believe them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is in Djakovica, March 1999. Where were you at that time, at the time of these alleged incidents, 24th of March through 11th May? I'm trying to find out how you're able to speak as authoritatively about these matters as you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from the 24th onwards, I was on the ground. I wasn't on the ground when these columns started forming. They started forming around the 1st of April. From the 1st of April until the 6th of April, every single day I was out in the area of Djeneral Jankovic and Vrbnica. These people from Djakovica could not reach the Vrbnica border crossing right away. I didn't see these people in Djakovica, but I did see people from all over Metohija who had arrived at the border, the border crossing towards Albania. This is the Vrbnica border crossing. There I spoke to them, I gave them assistance, I gave them medical assistance with my teams. We gave them what food we had, we brought diapers for the babies and anything else we were able to offer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You told us earlier that the alleged acts in paragraph (G) were committed not by Serb police but by criminals, and I think you told us that you -- you were in Pristina at that time, the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was in Pristina on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the distance between Pristina and Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance between Pristina and Djakovica via Prizren is 111 kilometres. There is another road which is 80 kilometres long, about 80 kilometres. It goes via Klina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because the time period in relation to both Prizren and Djakovica is relatively the same, so it's not clear to me how you had information about these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Robinson, I was on the ground. I spoke to large numbers of people, and I got this information from people who told me about it. I was also a member of the provincial council, and I know that this was not the policy we advocated. It was not possible. Individuals might have done such things, but not under orders from their superior command, because our policy was quite different. From the very first day, our policy was to escort these people, to get them to come back, as far as we were able to, and if not, to give them assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, let us clarify. As Mr. Robinson is not clear about where you were, whether you were in Pristina, Djakovica, Prizren, Djeneral Jankovic, and so on and so forth, when we say "on the ground," this means travelling in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, when Mr. Andric says he was on the ground, this means he was travelling. He lived in Pristina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's for Mr. Andric to explain. You may not believe it, but the questions I asked and the answers, I believe, strengthened your case. Proceed quickly. We are still working towards the first break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to say when somebody is going on an official trip, a business trip, they often say, "I'm going out on the ground." This is not usual in other languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Pristina, in Djakovica, in Prizren and Djeneral Jankovic and other places?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at the next count or, rather, paragraph (h)(ii). "In the place -- villages Meja, Korenica, a large number, not yet established, of civilians were separated off and executed." Is this the village of Meja where the NATO bombs hit?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of these events in Meja?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I've heard of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you do you know what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th of April, yes. I was on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible in any way from the information you have to claim that these people were killed by soldiers or policemen of the FRY or of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these people killed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were killed in a series of attacks by the NATO aviation on the convoy that was moving along the road. It lasted for almost two hours. It was not a single attack, it was several attacks on a large territory covering 30 or more kilometres, not just a kilometre or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's speed up. Were all the people who left their homes leaving the country or were some internally displaced temporarily?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not everyone who left their homes left the province. A large number of these people were internally displaced temporarily on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your tasks, and we have seen those documents in the staff, throughout the NATO aggression did you deal with these people?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 1st of April when we started with our mobile medical teams, escorting and assisting the columns that turned up and then later assisting internally displaced persons, up until the end of the war this was the only thing we did every day. We dealt with temporarily displaced persons and looked after them in every way; providing food, medical assistance, security, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a nutshell, you were assisting them.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you doing this on a daily basis or sporadically?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a daily basis, with several teams, all over the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I cannot ask you now about the entire territory, but would you give me some examples of this kind.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the most obvious example is the area of Podujevo municipality, the village of Sajkovac, the village of Svetlje, because in mid-April, I learned that in the area of Baklava Smrekovnica, the lake, and the village of Baklava, there were several thousand internally displaced people who needed assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right away, as soon as I found out about it, together with Selim Guxhufi and Faik Jashari, members of the provisional provincial council, I went out on the spot and I surveyed the situation and we immediately organised assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this assistance consist of?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first we had to feed those starving people. Then we had to provide accommodation, health care, security, and we did this very quickly. We managed to look after these people until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you now please play tab 5.12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It already started. It had started. You saw that it started. So who is the person we can see at the beginning of this clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This tab refers to -- here it is. Who is this man?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Selim Guxhufi, a member of the provisional provincial Executive Council, and he's an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our aim was to stabilise the situation everywhere in the municipality and all over the place so that the free life could be restarted and you'd be able to contribute first and foremost for your family and the closer relatives and the others. In cooperation with the -- or the organs of power, we can assure you a hundred per cent that the villages that I'm about to read out to you are going to be safe for you and your life is going to be safe and nobody's going to bother you or hurt you. "So with this group today and tomorrow, when everything's going to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be stabilised, we will return and register every family so that we have a more exact idea whether every member of the family is around, or if they are somewhere in villages or on the roads, they be found. So what I'm calling for is that you cooperate with us and we cooperate with you. "In the event of any dispute or disagreement, can you please tell us. Let us not have any disagreements so that nothing bad should happen to you or to us. We've come here with the best of intentions. We are here to assist you. We have got the agreement from the highest republican and provincial and municipal organs, and so you should cooperate with us by all means. Every grievance that you should encounter should be notified to us so that together we're able to resolve them. And given that there's an array of issues we have to sort out, and we have to talk to many other people on this score, I have to say that these villages which I have here in hand are villages to which you can return very freely. The others which I'm not about to read, they will also be liberated. There's an army. There's the police there. They do not know who you are, and there could be grave consequences. But the villages are, for example, Shtedim, Mirofc, Belofc, Sirfisi [phoen], Poljnica, Gladeko [phoen], Sibofc, Lower Sibofc, Dumoc [phoen], Radiovac [phoen] -- what does this mean? Shajkofc, Latovci, Balofc, Mirofc, Batllave, Dusija [phoen], Turnova, Taljabak, Shakove [phoen] -- is Shakove here? Luzani and Lug. "So as of today, these -- all of you can return to these villages, which means that the forces have been withdrawn from these villages. So from these villages. Latovci's here, Shajkofc's here, Radiojec [phoen] is here, Tomovci is here, Lower Sipos [phoen] is here. Trnava is also here. Lug, Shakove, Belo Polje, for example, is here. Brzac [phoen] is here, Trnava is here, Taljabak as well. Batllave as well. And then we're talking here about the place where there's a large concentration of people. "I am from Dubnica and I'm going to Glavnik. "So the state is ensuring your security. "That's what they told us. Let's wait and see. "And so you're going? "Yes, we've heard that and we're going to check it out. We don't know what's happened. "The dispensary here in Sajkovac village is starting to function. "This is a splendid thing. No, no around these two villages he is the only man responsible for the health of the province so he has provided two health care stations, two dispensaries which will work in Svetlje and Sajkovac. All the villagers have the opportunity of getting a check-up, getting medicines, and being treated. "A large number of these people have nothing to eat. Their food reserves have been exhausted. Through your staff is there any chance, please, for the people to get some humanitarian aid as far as is actually possible? "Yes, but probably not today. "I don't mean today but tomorrow. "For tomorrow certainly. For tomorrow certainly. There will be some tomorrow, it's too late today. "The police and the army are ensuring your security in those villages of the Podujevo community. Are you going to return to your houses? "For the time being, we think so. "And the other villagers? Have you got somewhere you can go to? "No, we're out there in the straw. There's no room here. Everything's full. We've been outdoors. Everybody's out in the open. There's no -- nowhere to go. We're more concerned about the children, not about ourselves. But it's only the children we're most concerned about. "Tomorrow the humanitarian dispensary will be working. Let's wait and see. There will be some food. Let's see. We need something to eat. We have to wait and see. "We've been -- we've been around the mountains for about a whole month with nothing at all, and we're nearing the end of our tether. "All we need -- from Grasnica we've been here walking on foot from Pristina to Podujevo and all along we could have made use of a bus or something of this sort but we've been forced to be on foot all the time. We just don't know. "I've been through two wars. This is the second war. We don't know what kind of war this is. What are we talking about here? We dare not return. Who should we protect ourselves from, from the bombardment here, the fighting here? We are upset about the children, these little children, and that's why we're here. The elderly have been through this, but we're most concerned about the children. That's all I have to say."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how much longer is this tape? Mr. Milosevic, how much longer is the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic is inaudible because of the sound of the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Forty minutes? If it's 40 minutes, no, I'm not having that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been shortened a lot. Look here, Nis, Podujevo. They are moving north towards the interior, not towards the border.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Is this the Podujevo community? "Why have you left your houses? "There is a war and we were forced to leave. "Are you returning to your own houses? "Yes. "Are you happy to be returning home? "Certainly we are. "Are you fearing the bombardment? "The bombardment, the children are too scared. "We -- we are here on the orders of the chairman of the provincial authority to bring you supplies, to distribute flour, rice, staples which are elementary and most necessary to help the people. We are here to discuss these problems and we believe that it will be resolved very, very soon. And you should be aware that the main reason for all of this is the NATO bombardment over the whole of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Kosovo. Regardless of who we're talking about, children or the elderly or women. I suppose that you agree with this. "Yes, certainly. "Everything that the members of the provisional Albanian government of Kosovo has said, what is your comment on this?"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is enough. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to require that this video is played in full. Being started, I have a reason for this. I require it to be played in full at some stage, it's better that it's played in full now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will explain that in cross-examination, Your Honour, and if necessary, I'll take the time in cross-examination, but this tape should be played in full now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I think you have to explain it now, because my view is that what we've seen is sufficiently representative of the point that he has to make. How much longer do we have to complete it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can interrupt it. I gave the entire tape so that everyone can use it. We can interrupt it now and I will move on in order to save time. As you yourself have said, this is enough to illustrate what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, of course I must have regard to your cross-examining, and you have a right to cross-examine. You believe that there is material in the rest of the tape on which you would want to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed there is. I'm quite happy if we -- I think it's probably better if we have it all, but I'm quite happy if we reach the end of page -- or halfway down page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's continue to halfway down page 8. We're going to continue to halfway down page 8. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Two days later, the president of the Executive Council, they said peacefully you should leave your homes. Where are we going? We don't know. Then we came to Sajkovac. We were there for four days. We left there and we were in the woods for almost two weeks. "Tell me, were you frightened by the bombing? "Of course. Everyone was frightened, not just me. Whether I'm Albanian or Serb or Macedonian or American, everyone is frightened. Even Americans are frightened of bombing. "But what are you afraid of? "Of some bombing that may be coming into my building. I have neighbours, I have. There are 15 families there, all with children. Look, there are children, four children. "And tell me, did you have problems with the police? "Never. I'm a lawyer by profession, and I have never had any problems with the police, never, never. (He shows documents and a business card.) This is my business card. I was born here and my grandfather and great grandfather. My grandfather has a house in the middle of the town of Podujevo and we have never had problems and we never will have. "Tell me, how did you decide to return home? "This is how we decided: Yesterday when there was that, you know, we are always frightened. They are shooting there. And where they are shooting they were not in the vicinity but we came out and left in the direction of Pristina and today in the morning a large column set off. "You said they were shooting. Who was shooting? "I don't know whether it was the police shooting, whether it was soldiers shooting, whether someone else was shooting, you know. And we, a large column, set off, maybe 150.000 people, maybe 100.000, maybe 50.000, I couldn't count them, but a large column and we set off in that column. When we reached Pristina the police stopped us. He said those who are from Podujevo, the Podujevo area, who have a permanent place of residence in Podujevo and the surrounding villages, you are to go to Podujevo. And they escorted us to 200 metres, to the way out, almost to Devet Jugovica. We got to Podujevo and we turned on the indicator, turned towards the centre when someone in civilian clothing came out and says, Where are you off to then? I say this way, he says, Let me have a check, then, so we can see. Then he had a talk - I don't know who he was talking with - he said go straight towards Sajkovac. "As we see, the state organs are here, so the state organs were enabling you to return to your houses. "Yes, we have to return, we have to return. I don't want to live in someone else's house. "And can we tell the criminals of NATO from here as witnesses ourselves but bombs don't choose between ethnic groups. "No, they don't choose any ethnic groups. Not Albanians, not Serbs, not Montenegrins, not Romas, not anyone. "So what can we tell the criminals of NATO? "We shall tell them to settle and all Albanians are for settling the Kosovo crisis peacefully for everyone. Not only for Serbs and Albanians, for me. What is the use of settling it for me when my neighbour does not live as he should or is afraid to live with me, for example? "Shall we tell the criminals of NATO to get out of here? "Well, there are other organs that will say that. "We as ordinary people. "As ordinary people, I would like this to be settled peacefully for the good of everyone, whoever has a good heart and a good opinion for every ethnicity. "But not -- "Not for bombing. Not for bombing. I am not for that. And most of my brothers and relations who are here are not for bombing. Who is going to gain from bombing? Who will gain? No one. For people to die for no purpose. "Who will benefit from bombing? "No one. People die for no purpose. We welcome -- we wish you a safe journey back home. "What's your last name? "Rexhep Fusa, from Podujevo. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "Do you want to return to your homes? "Yes. "So the state has enabled you to return to your own homes. "Yes. We shall return for us to work and live. What can I say?" "Look, Yugoslavia and NATO are at war and Albanians are paying the price. You see just what disaster this is among the people, and children and old people are suffering. I haven't had anything to eat for two days now, nothing at all. We were in the woods for three weeks, so we have no comments. "And whose fault is it? "I am no expert. I can't tell you who is to blame for this. "Do you think that many people suffered, were killed, many children? "We've been in the woods for three weeks. "But Serbs and Albanians are suffering together. "I'm telling you. "I'm very sincere. We spent three weeks in the woods, no chance to hear what's going on, and therefore I'm sorry that people were killed someplace else, people who are innocent, but I'm speaking personally about what I see here. Everything that we can see here, these houses, these children, this crowd. I have no comments. What else can I tell you?" "You see, a part of humanitarian aid which you can see here is being unloaded. We have provided this for the citizens of Podujevo. We will provide more and more of such aid every day. This is in coordination with the organs of Serbia and the interim government of Kosovo and Metohija. "A little earlier we had an opportunity to talk to the citizens receiving humanitarian aid, because this is not taking place just today. We've been doing this since the 19th of this month, and I can tell you openly that they are very satisfied and grateful to the authorities. They told us that they would become active in order to accomplish all the tasks set to them by the authorities. They're ready to cooperate to the maximum extent, and they're very pleased with everything that has been done since they returned to their villages and houses and towns. "I would like to say that the aid you see here is very diverse. It includes food, which is needed right now. It also includes sanitary supplies. The majority of it is rice, but there's also sugar, flour, pasta, other types of food supplies, and I think that the citizens will welcome it. We are also working on opening in the city several bakeries. One is in operation already and bakes 2 to 3.000 loaves of bread every day. And in a way, in a complex situation such as this one, we will ensure at least that the minimum needs of the citizens in Podujevo area are met." "This has to continue throughout the entire period. People have to receive supplies because they are very tired from everything that's been going on. They have travelled quite a lot. They're tired. "But now you've returned to your homes. "Well, people are still afraid. The majority has not returned, but once they hear that things have calmed down, they will return soon. I received a permit enabling me to move freely about the town and then we'll see. I don't know what will happen next, but so far so good. "What's your name? "Sabri Berisha. "From Podujevo? "Yes, from Podujevo. I'm a tyre repairman. My workshop was burned down, but God willing, we shall build a better one, a new one. As long as there are no problems, we'll be able to carry on. We'll see. "Thank you." "This is a recording which we had today in the village of Podujevo --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the next one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't really follow this. I believed that they would stop after we see the footage that Mr. Nice wanted to see. I don't mind seeing the entire footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is this the point where we should stop?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to stop here, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We finished off the tab, tab 5.12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can tabs 5.11 and 5.12 be made exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, Dr. Andric: We could see you in this tape talking to citizens, you and several colleagues of yours. When I say "colleagues," by that I'm trying to say that these are the people who are also members of the provisional Executive Council of the government of Kosovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are these people? They mostly spoke in Albanian, but we also saw that some words were uttered in Serbian. So who are these people who mostly spoke to Albanian citizens?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were three members of the provincial Executive Council, Jashari, Guxhufi, and Ismaili. Let me just mention that Ismaili was killed after the end of the war upon returning to his village precisely because he was a member of the provisional Executive Council. The -- two of these people were also members of the provincial staff for humanitarian issues whose chairman I was. They went with me in the field all the time, assisting everyone and carrying out the activities that we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, first of all, please establish who filmed this footage and how were they compiled. And I would also like to know who the journalist was who asked the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this is just one portion of the footage that was recorded at the time about the activities and events taking place in Kosovo, but perhaps the witness can tell us more about what you just asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, please tell us what you know about who recorded this.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This footage consists of several recorded events. There was a cameraman who always accompanied me whenever I went out in the field. I always took him with me to record our activities. So there was a journalist from Television S and cameraman Boro Danilovic who always accompanied me and recorded events. This was recorded in the second half of April 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point we saw the road sign saying "Direction Nis," which showed that the column was moving in the direction of Nis, therefore away from the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These people from Podujevo and Podujevo area were moving towards the administrative border with Serbia. They were moving towards north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have the transcript here reflecting your words to the effect that the infirmary is being opened in two villages. Was it really in two villages?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In two villages, Sajkovac and Svetlje. On that day we even opened an infirmary in Glogovac. On the 29th of April, 1999. These infirmaries remained open until the end of the war, providing daily medical assistance to anyone who needed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It is stated here as Selim Guxhufi stated, "All villagers can attend infirmary, receive medication --"

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the health care was provided free to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they receive medication right away?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can see here that you promised that you would bring the trucks, trucks with food the following day because Guxhufi told you that the people were hungry. Did you indeed send the trucks with food the following day?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And until the end of the war, we provided full food supplies to these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present there when the man said, "How can we protect ourselves? Bombing here, bombing there. I feel sorry for our children. We've been through a lot." Was he trying to say that they were bombing the entire area?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was present there, and that's what he was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here in the transcript we can't discern who is speaking, but I think it must be Guxhufi saying that the aid has arrived and is being distributed. At any rate, this is just one illustration of your activities, and it involves this particular operation. In my information, it is stated here that there were around 40.000 Albanians gathered in that area where you were at the time distributing and sending aid.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one moment there were about 40.000 of them. We sent them to 16 villages where we were able to find accommodation for them, and they continued living in their villages until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since internally displaced persons received food, assistance, and so on, tell us, do you have any statistical figures reflecting that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a daily basis, aid was distributed. Let me give you some examples. On the 3rd of May, 1999, in Vucitrn, there were several thousand internally displaced persons of Albanian ethnicity. We provided housing for them, and on the first day we distributed 15.000 kilogrammes of food to them and found accommodation for them in the neighbouring villages, Kitica [phoen], Smrekovnica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In tab 12, gentlemen, we can see a table showing the supplies that were distributed through the provincial staff, precisely this staff that the witness is describing right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please let us comment -- please comment this table very briefly.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting on the 15th of April, 1999, until the 31st of May, we distributed over 300.000 kilogrammes of food and about 60.000 kilogrammes of sanitary supplies. This is just part of the food that we distributed through our staff for humanitarian issues. This does not include the aid distributed through the Yugoslav Red Cross and later on through the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this food was distributed to internally displaced Albanians. The question is not so much whether Serb Albanians did good works in distributing food to those who were displaced. The question raised by the indictment is how these people became displaced. What was the cause of their displacement. That is what should be investigated. Nothing really turns on the good works that were done while they were displaced. The issue is how did they come to be displaced. Generally the indictment says that the Serbs were responsible for the displacement. That's the issue. So evidence of the good works done by Serbs to them while they were displaced is not taking us much further in dealing with the precise issues raised by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I hope that these illustrations, although I do not think that things can be generalised, but I hope that these illustrations show clearly that people said they were fleeing from bombing. There were places in Kosovo and Metohija that were subjected to more severe bombing and those subjected to less severe bombing, but this is a relative notion because the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija was bombed 24 hours a day for 78 days. People fled the areas that were hit the most. There were also areas where there were conflicts, especially in certain regions. These were conflicts between our forces and the KLA, and people also fled those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is you concentrate the evidence on the reasons for the displacement, but proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, what were the reasons? Please tell us. You had many contacts with these people, together with other members of the Executive Council; Guxhufi, Jashari and Ibrahimi. So please tell us, how did these people become displaced? It was very nice of you to help them, you heard what Mr. Robinson just said, but why did they become displaced?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated several times that the exodus started the day NATO began its aggression and bombing. They left their towns and villages and went to places they believed were safer. In addition to that, there were also places where there was severe fighting going on between the members of the so-called KLA and the army or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police, and the population also fled those areas and went to calmer regions. However, I have to say that the internally displaced persons were not internally displaced throughout the entire 78 days. They were displaced perhaps for 15 or 10 days, and then they would return to their homes. In Sajkovac, we only initially distributed the food to the internally displaced persons until we found housing for them. These -- this involves 40.000 people who were displaced only initially, and later on we were able to take them back to their villages, and then we provided assistance to them there. There were only a small -- there was only a small number of residents who was unable to return to their homes, so we housed them in temporary accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us take a look at tab 13. This previous one was tab 12.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The refugees who for months were running around returned and began their normal life, and as promised yesterday, the members of the -- of the provisional council, Selim Jashari [as interpreted] and Selim Guxhufi, the first mobile medical units were installed here and they will serve the inhabitants of this -- of this region and provide the medicaments and the medical aid for everybody, including the children. All of this is done with a view towards -- towards surviving the NATO agreement which would basically come to be illustrated through the popular saying that you can judge the best days if you look at the sky in the morning." "From the establishment of the staff of humanitarian affairs and internally displaced persons on the 19th April, over 200 tons of food and 20 tons of toiletries were distributed. "We have to deal with internally displaced persons because that was required by the situation on the ground. We had initially over 50.000 displaced persons, and their problem was dealt with successfully. Then the problem of Vucitrn, Glogova, and ever new places occurred. However, we managed to deal with them successfully. "In order to be as operative as we can, we in the Kosovo staff formed area staffs and municipal staffs, such as in Podujevo, which helped us deal with the problems of Sajkovac and other places. The principle of the Kosovo staff, the guiding principle of our staff is to help people and distribute humanitarian aid regardless of ethnicity. So we distributed it to Albanians, Serbs, the Gorani, the Roma, everybody who needed it. We didn't forget any of the three ethnic communities. We distributed, however, a certain portion of that food to specific ethnic communities. For instance, we drove one truck today to Mamusa, and we distributed a truck full of food to Egyptians today. Yesterday, we drove a truck full of food and toiletries to the Gora municipality, and we took care in the same way of the ethnic community of the Roma. And I believe that all ethnic communities specifically can be pleased with our work. "One of the burning problems is health care provision in the areas where displaced persons are located and where persons are trying to return home. We believe that we have done all in our power in cooperation with the health care centre of the Kosovo district and with the Kosovo health care institute. I believe we did our best. Wherever there was a large concentration of displaced persons, we did not allow any epidemics to develop and the epidemiological situation has always been under control. We distributed medicine wherever it was needed. There were mobile medical teams constantly on the ground from the health care centre of the Kosovo district that went into the field every day. Today they are in the Glogovac municipality where there are rampant problems. Glogovac has not had a steady water supply for some time, so there is still -- there is still a threat of an epidemic. I believe the mobile teams of the provincial health centre institute and the health care centre of Kosovo will resolve the problem. "If we can't find any other solution to supply water to Glogovac, we will have to disinfect the local wells that exist there. That problem has to be placed under control to avoid a major epidemic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Dr. Andric, apart from looking after internally displaced persons, was it one of your obligations to work for returning life to normalcy in all areas, to prevent contagion, epidemics, provision of food, water, restoring water supply? Are all these problems that you had to deal with this in period where bombs were falling 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo teams for health care were on the ground every day and we were trying to do all that we would normally be doing in peacetime; distribution of consumer goods, water supply, restoration of communications between towns and cities, because -- although that was a very difficult task because there was a lot of destruction -- people needed to be provided with continued health care. Supply of electricity had to continue uninterrupted. Briefly, everything that normal life implies. We tried whatever we could. We did our best to normalise life in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of those internally displaced people remained displaced, but large numbers were put up in provisional accommodation and a certain number of people were convinced, after all, to return to their homes. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever we could tell people that their homes were safe, we told them to return. However, the largest number of people could not return because war operations were under way in the areas concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute. What war operations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the areas where we were present, there was fighting between the regular police and the army on the one hand, and the so-called KLA, the terrorist gangs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. You said those terrorist gangs were active there. So is that what your colleague Guxhufi was trying to explain to that crowd of Albanians in the video clip when he was holding a map and telling them to which villages it was safe to return and which they should avoid because fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Sixteen villages were safe for them to return to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you are concluding now and that's why I haven't taken the adjournment, because we are past the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have a number of questions pending, Mr. Robinson. I've really been doing my level best to finish before the end of this session, but a number of questions are still left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber is appreciative of that effort. We will now take the adjournment for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I note that tab 5.13, 5.14, as well as tab 12 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, let us try to cover some more exhibits. I will not quote them in detail here. Just briefly look at tab 13. It relates to measures you took to normalise the conditions of life, to provide the necessary medicines and vaccines for children, for babies that had not been vaccinated yet. But then in tab 14, you see a number of subitems from which we can see that there is a serious problem of water supply, water testing and provision of potable water. Tell me, why was the water problem so serious?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the installations for production and filtering of water were seriously damaged by NATO bombing, in Pristina and Gnjilane specifically. In Gnjilane, for instance, there was no fresh drinking water for over a month, and in Pristina there was no potable water for a long time because these installations had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 14.1, 2 to 5, we letters from the institute for health care which deal primarily with restoring normal life conditions. What efforts were made to restore normalcy, and did you manage to restore a normal water supply to these areas of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were problems in every area, especially in Pristina because it's a large city, and in Gnjilane. But I would particularly like to emphasise the problem of Glogovac where the water supply system had occasionally suffered for problems even before the war because the water pipes were obsolete. And during the war, we had to provide fresh water to civilians from the existing wells, and every day we would bring cisterns, water tanks to Glogova and distribute fresh water to the population there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us not waste any more time on this. I would like documents under tab 14 tendered in their entirety, 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, just -- in tab 14.1, this is the professor, this is the professor's signature. The Federal Institute for Preventive Medicine, and the first sentence is, "The vital water treatment facilities in Sajkovac and Badovac have been damaged by enemy airstrikes." That might be how this aspect of the evidence could be relevant, but simply to have evidence of what the professor did as a doctor in relation to refugees and to people who were injured, to help them, is not so relevant. But if the water treatment facilities were damaged by air strikes and as a result of that your case is that people -- the Albanians had to flee, then that's a different matter. So I'm not certain whether that is -- whether anything can be made of that, but I just thought I'd bring that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this, Mr. Robinson. Maybe you didn't quite notice it while you were looking at another document, but I just asked the witness, since these tabs contain a number of documents relating to measures taken by authorities to normalise life in many areas in Kosovo and Metohija, I asked him why water supply was a problem, and he answered that the water supply was a particular problem in Pristina and in another town because NATO strikes damaged a number of water supply and water treatment facilities, and it took superhuman efforts for them to provide fresh water to the population in a very large area, to conduct medical examination of a large number of people, to prevent epidemics, to provide immunisation, and that's why I required these documents to be tendered into evidence. So I would appreciate if you would admit into evidence tabs 13 and 14 containing a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, you have already explained that you accommodated some of these displaced persons in houses or elsewhere, but some did go to Albania. Can you explain this? In spite of all your care and assistance and the supplies you provided, some of them went to Albania. Why?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened in the Glogovac area, where we were active throughout the war, and this was where the so-called KLA, the terrorists, were especially active, and all the local inhabitants went to Glogovac where they could have more peace and security. In mid-May, about 8.000 internally displaced Albanians turned up in an area near the Celinac river. We went there and began our usual procedure of taking care of their needs, and they remained there for quite some time. Toward the end of the war, for reasons I cannot explain, some of these Albanians went. I assume part of them went to their villages, but some of them went to the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the NATO aggression on Kosovo and Metohija, did humanitarian aid arrive from abroad? And let me add another question to that: How was it distributed if it arrived?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, humanitarian did arrive from abroad. The first large shipment arrived from Greece through an organisation called European Perspective. It was a gift from the Greek government. There were 200 tons of different foodstuffs. It arrived on the 27th of April. In mid-May, the international or, rather, the office of the ICRC for Yugoslavia brought in a large convoy containing food. There were 13 trucks, trailer trucks, and all this humanitarian assistance was distributed according to need. Our only rule when distributing it was the need of the population for this humanitarian aid regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In tab 5.15, we can see how humanitarian aid arrived, and here we can see that you provide an explanation, saying that it was being distributed non-selectively to everyone who needed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm asking you, I want this tab to be introduced but I have described what it contains. Perhaps we can skip over it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we should hear it. I think we should see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Could you please then play tab 5.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is you, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, leaving the clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the humanitarian aid from Greece?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is not the first time humanitarian aid has come from Greece. Could you tell us something more about it? "Well, in the past week this is the third time humanitarian aid has come from friendly Greece. It's the third convoy. There were 11 trucks in this last convoy, with some 220 tons of goods, mostly foodstuffs. Humanitarian aid will be contributed to all those in this area who need it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is tab 5.15. I've already described its contents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. This is the next clip. Just a moment, please. Could you stop it now. This is not the tab in question. This is the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, apart from Serbs and Montenegrins and other non-Albanians in general who were fleeing Kosovo towards central Serbia, were there any Albanians among them fleeing towards central Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A part of the Albanians fled in the direction of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does this tell us? What can you say on the basis of this? I don't want to put a leading question to you. If they were fleeing towards central Serbia, I assume they were not fleeing from the state authorities.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, because if they were fleeing the government authorities, why would they be rushing into their arms? It's evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from residential buildings, did NATO target other civilian facilities?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from these convoys, they targeted bridges, means of transportation, water processing plants, telecommunication plants, electrical transformer plants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's so many of them one tends to get relaxed about leading questions but the question, "Did NATO target other civilian facilities?" is clearly leading but I'll deal with it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can 5.15 be an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, you said that they targeted other facilities. Specifically did you have any knowledge as to how a bus full of passengers was targeted travelling on the Nis-Pristina road near the village of Luzani? This is just an example.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on the 1st of May at 1300 hours. The NATO Air Force and the Lab river in Luzani hit a bus full of passengers, and on that occasion 39 passengers were killed. Twenty-nine of them were Albanians and ten were Serbs. There were also 12 passengers seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question that you asked was how a bus full of passengers was targeted, and you got an answer. Are you saying, Professor, that that busload of passengers was actually targeted by NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Robinson, the bus was hit. There is no doubt that it was done by NATO bombs. I assume intentionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that you were asked and which you answered affirmatively was related to the bus being targeted. Do you have any specific evidence that the hitting of the bus by the NATO bomb was the result of a specific targeting of the bus by NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of evidence I could have, but I know for certain that the NATO Air Force fired and that a bus full of passengers was hit on the bridge. This was a civilian bus belonging to the Nis Ekspres company travelling on the regular line, and it contained mostly Albanians who were travelling, I assume, from Podujevo to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, in tab 15 in the clip showing this bus, let me first put a question to you. This was a civilian bus on a regular line?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the regular route it took, and you assumed that they were travelling from one place to another. Of course, if this is a regular service --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused can just give the evidence, if he likes. We've now had leading question, assumption made by the witness. It's up to the accused, but none of these questions are likely to be of any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you'll have to rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, would you please put on the ELMO the photographs from tab 15. Dr. Andric, was this the bus running on the regular service route?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it hit on the bridge, and were several dozen passengers killed? Was it hit by a plane belonging to the NATO pact?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be assumed that the bus was hit because it was not targeted or because it was targeted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He can't answer that. He can't answer that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the broader area around that bus on that bridge, was there any other facility that might have been a target for the bombing?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that area very well, and I was on the spot half an hour after the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the vicinity are there any military facilities, any barracks, or any kind of centre near the bridge on which that bus was hit?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The village of Luzani is nearby, with only small family houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is nothing else nearby?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Andric. Will you tell me briefly now, did any foreign representatives visit Kosovo and Metohija during the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I remember that in mid-May, in the second half of May, the chief of the office for Yugoslavia of the ICRC, Mr. Dominique Diffours visited Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have a look at tab 16, please, and I'll put my next question. What places did they want to visit in Kosovo and Metohija and what did they see on the ground, these foreign representatives?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please play tab 5.16.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Professor Vukasin Andric and the chairman of the Committee for Humanitarian Issues, Veljko Odalovic, talked today with the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross for the FRY, Dominique Diffours. During the talks it was emphasised that in these difficult times for the FRY, when the entire country and the entire population are exposed to round-the-clock airstrikes and aid is needed from humanitarian organisations. To that end, possibilities were reviewed to reactivate the Red Cross subcommittee in Pristina which is supposed to cover the area of Kosovo and Metohija. It was emphasised that aid by our humanitarian organisations had been offered to everyone regardless of their ethnicity, religion, or race from the first day of the NATO aggression. The provisional Executive Council and Red Cross reacted every time and provided necessary aid to civilians who were endangered by the aggression of the NATO alliance. It was said that all international humanitarian organisations left the area when the aggression started. However, it is encouraging that some, like the ICRC, are returning to Kosovo and Metohija again. Almost two months of ceaseless airstrikes have left severe consequences on civilians since many facilities were destroyed and many people have been displaced. It was agreed that in the future cooperation between the ICRC, the Red Cross of Kosovo and Metohija and state organs will be based on joint assistance to the threatened population. It was emphasised that the ICRC will provide adequate basic staples and other need -- other things that are needed to overcome the humanitarian problems in Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now pass on to the next tab. Yes, please continue because we will comment both clips together in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Svend Robinson, a member of the New Democratic Party, which has 21 MPs in the Canadian parliament and which is against the NATO aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, visited Kosovo and Metohija today. Accompanied by members of the interim Executive Council, Robinson visited the village of Sajkovac in Podujevo municipality. The local authorities informed the Canadian MP of the current situation in the area. Robinson said that he had come to the FRY to acquaint himself first-hand with the situation, the consequences of the NATO bombing, and the Yugoslav government's position regarding a peaceful and political resolution of the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija. The Canadian MP also visited a bridge near Luzani where the NATO aggressor killed about 50 innocent civilians who were travelling to Pristina in a Nis Ekspres bus on the 1st of May. In the village of Staro Gracko he could also see first-hand the NATO aggressors democratic effects.
