He visited the household of the Jankovic family, where two members were killed by the NATO aggressors, as well as the house of the Dinic family where four-year-old Dragana Dinic was killed. Svend Robinson also visited a site with several unexploded cluster bombs when he was able to see that there were only civilian buildings in the area and no military or police forces nearby. "At the clinical hospital centre in Pristina, centre director Dr. Rade Grbic informed Robinson of how victims of the NATO aggressor's attacks were treated, regardless of their religious or ethnic background. Svend Robinson said that he had come to our country in order to see for himself the consequences of the NATO bombing and to hear our position regarding a possible political solution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the NATO bombing is relevant, but it is relevant in a particular way. The NATO bombing is not in and of itself a part of the case. It is relevant, in my view, principally in two ways. It's relevant if you are saying that as a result of the NATO bombing the charges in the indictment that relate to Albanians fleeing their homes and which the indictment attributes to the activities of Serbs is actually the result of the bombing. That's one way in which it is relevant. It's also relevant in this way: If you're saying that the charges -- some of the charges in the indictment which are attributed to Serbs were a response to the bombing. I understand that part of your case is that NATO was in collusion with the KLA. So if some of the activities -- if you're saying that some of the activities attributable to the Serbs were in fact responsive to, were in fact defensive action in response to NATO bombing, then that is obviously relevant. But the NATO bombing is not in and of itself a part of the case. NATO is not charged. So two principal ways: One, defensive, self-defence; and secondly, in relation to charges concerning refugees. I've allowed you to lead the evidence about NATO bombing even when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it is not clearly related to any of those issues, because the issues are very intertwined, they're so closely interrelated. But I have to give you a warning that you will not be allowed to continue leading evidence about the NATO bombing unless it is specifically relevant, and I gave you two examples of how it could be relevant, because we don't have time to waste in this case. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just continue. Just continue. I don't want to have another long intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to correct -- I'm not going to go into a long comment, but what was shown here and will be shown here and everything that has been shown so far clearly indicates the cause and consequence relation that exists between the bombing and the fleeing of people from Kosovo. You know that hundred thousand Serbs also fled Kosovo. So if Serbs expelled Albanians, why would they expel Serbs as well? Percentage-wise, the number of Serbs fleeing Kosovo was greater than the number of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, we saw that a Canadian MP even took photographs of the fragmentation bomb that was dropped in Kosovo and Metohija. Not just there but also in Nis, in front of the clinical and hospital centre in Nis. So please tell us, what did you discuss with these international representatives? Is it clear that they were unaware of the fact that such bombs were used?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Canadian MP wanted to go to the village where a couple was killed and a four-year-old girl, and he was able to see for himself that between the 11th and the 12th of May that village was hit with cluster bombs. He even took pictures of cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they want to visit some other places that were of special interest too? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to go and see villages and see how people live in villages. They toured several villages in Podujevo municipality and were able to see for themselves that people carried on their regular calm way of life, carrying out their daily activities. In addition to that, they wanted to tour the hospital centre, and Mr. Robinson wanted to see the civilian victims of Serb police and army. I quoted his words verbatim. I told him he could enter any ward he wanted, any clinic he wanted within that hospital centre and that there was simply no such victims, no such patients there. He refused to go in and visit the hospital centre. And towards the end you were able to see that he also toured the Serbian Orthodox cemetery in Pristina which was also hit with two NATO rounds which destroyed about a dozen of tombstones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime in May, and you can be more accurate if you know, you also had a visit by Sergio De Mello, who was the chief of the UN mission for humanitarian issues. Do you remember what they wanted to see? Where did you take them, and what can you tell us about the visit of the special envoy of the UN Secretary-General, Sergio De Mello?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he visited the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija. My associates and I met him. He wanted to see the destroyed facilities in Gnjilane, mostly civilian industrial facilities, the administrative building of the construction company, the building of the automobile association, the building of the transportation company Kosmet Prevoz, also their workshops. After that, we went to Pristina. On the following day he visited Kacanik and Urosevac. That was on the 21st of May, 1999. He arrived on the 20th of May. On the 22nd of May, I personally went with Mr. De Mello to visit the entire Podujevo area. He was able to see for himself that the population was taken care of there, that they lived in their homes. After that we went to Prizren, Djakovica, Decani and Pec. It was a Sunday. I remember that well. In the afternoon, Mr. De Mello left Kosovo and Metohija and went to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have here under tab 5.18 video footage depicting the visit of Sergio De Mello, and I think the witness has described it sufficiently. However, if you insist that the clip be played, that's fine. This is tab 5.18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. If you don't want the clip to be played, it will not be played. We want to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I simply asked if it was necessary to play it in order for it to be admitted into evidence. If it is, then let's play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was an issue, I recall, in the Prosecution case involving I think their second witness, Mr. Spargo, who had a large number of videotapes, I think some three hours and 40 minutes, and the Court on that occasion ruled that they could just as well view the videos outside court hours as use up court time in the viewing of them. Perhaps that would be an acceptable solution in this case where we have spent some considerable time looking at the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So there is that precedent. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is probably the first time that we have seen -- it may be the first time that we've seen Andjelkovic, so I think perhaps -- it won't take very long, perhaps we ought to have a look at it if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do we need to see all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's possible to do it without seeing all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It can't be stopped?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's only three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It isn't long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's three minutes. All right. Let's play it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not long at all. We can play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, three minutes. Let's play it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's even less than three.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The Under-Secretary of the UN Interagency Mission for Humanitarian Issues, Mr. Sergio De Mello, and his associates, who are in Kosovo and Metohija, were met by the members of the provisional Executive Council, Professor Vukasin Andric and Guljbehar Sabovic as well as the head of the Kosovo-Morava District, Predrag Kovacevic. "The head of the district informed those in attendance of the consequences of the NATO bombing the previous day in Gnjilane. "He informed them that garages, workshops and the factory canteen were demolished in yesterday's bombing of the Mladost agricultural complex. Three female workers were killed within that same compound. "The construction company's Binacka Morava facilities were hit and two workers killed. "The Kosmet Prevoz company was shelled with four rounds yesterday. The Automobile Club, which began to work only last year, was completely demolished. "The water supply grid was damaged in NATO bombings and Gnjilane residents were without water for a total of 15 days. "The total damage in Gnjilane is enormous as it was solely civilian buildings that were targetted. Since the beginning of NATO bombing, in addition to the aforementioned casualties, more than 60 civilians have been wounded. Fifteen people were wounded in yesterday's attack alone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just need to verify something, Mr. Robinson. It was probably my own omission, but I'm not sure whether you admitted into evidence tab 12, which described the aid distributed through this staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just several more questions, Dr. Andric. Did you remain in Kosovo and Metohija after the war?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until what time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 25th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us briefly, what was the security situation like for Serbs in Pristina after the KFOR's arrival? You were in Pristina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did KFOR protect you at all; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the arrival of KFOR forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and before the arrival, we hoped that they would be able to protect not just Serbs but all non-Albanians. An unprecedented persecution of non-Albanian population, including Serb population, began. They started raiding apartments, looting, beating people, killing them, kidnapping them, simply a terrible hunt on people began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you continue working at the hospital centre in Pristina and why did you stop working there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stopped working there on the 25th of June, 1999, because it was impossible to continue under those circumstances. Already on the 20th of June, 1999, in the courtyard of the hospital centre we saw an armoured battalion of KFOR, and we were very pleased. We hoped that they would be able to protect us and the entire institution. However, on the 21st of June, the doctors, professors, Albanians who had previously left their jobs came back, asking to be allowed in. On the 22nd of June, they forced their way into the clinics and the medical school. Not just them but some people that I saw then for the first time in my life. They were tanned. They had tanned faces, and I realised that they were the former KLA members who had donned on civilian clothing. The unprecedented harassment began, and we continued working under those circumstances. On the 22nd of June, they killed Professor Lekovic from the faculty of economy and his two associates, who were beaten beyond recognition. Several days after that Mr. Tomanovic, director of the surgical hospital, was killed. He operated on a very large number of people, many of them Albanians. We tried working under those conditions. Everybody was threatened. Everybody received death threats, and we were sure that they would proceed with their threats until they killed us all. We managed to survive there until Friday the end of June, and on that Friday we left the institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your mother-in-law was killed during NATO bombing. Were any other of your relatives killed during the aggression or after KFOR arrival?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 22nd of June in the evening my wife's brother was killed. He went to visit the apartment of his younger brother from which his younger brother had been evicted by the KLA members. He went there with his wife and his child. It was evening, and when he got there he found a note on the door and it had the following Albanian words, the witness quotes in Albanian, which translated into Serbian, means "This is KLA's apartment. Do not enter. It has been mined." He went to report this to the British members of the KFOR and was killed some 20 metres further away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of anybody else who was killed? Was there another colleague of yours, professor or doctor who was kidnapped and killed after the arrival of the international forces?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned Professor Tomanovic and Professor Lekovic from the faculty of economy. On the day of the flag, in the centre of Pristina, that was on the 28th of November, 1999, Professor Basic, who taught at the civil engineering factory, was killed. In August, Dr. Slate Grigurjevic [phoen], a renowned paediatrician, was killed in his practice, private practice. And on the 26th of February, 2000, I think, in the centre of Gnjilane, a renowned gynaecologist, Dr. Vasic, was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, how and when did you leave Pristina and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Pristina on the 25th of June, 1999, in the afternoon, escorted by the International Red Cross staff, and I went to central Serbia. That was the only way for me to leave the territory of Kosovo and Metohija safely because I had received death threats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live now and what is your job now?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I currently live in Kosovska Mitrovica. I am a full-time tenured professor of the medical school of the Pristina University, now Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. temporarily relocated to Kosovska Mitrovica. Unfortunately, this is the only university in the so-called free Europe and free world working in immigration. In addition to that, I work in the otorhinolaryngology ward of the Kosovska Mitrovica hospital, which is the only hospital where Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija can be treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, I have just one more question for you. You've lived -- you lived in Pristina for a long time. Do you know any Serb from Pristina - your neighbour, colleague, friend, anyone - who was not ethnically cleansed from Pristina under the sponsorship of the international forces? Do you know of a single case?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until March of last year, perhaps I did know some cases of people who lived under extremely difficult, undignified conditions, as though in concentration camp. That's how they lived in Pristina. After the last year's pogrom, no such people remain in Pristina any more. Prior to that, they lived in a building. All of them were concentrated in just one building that was called the U-programme building, and nowadays the only city open to the Serbs is Kosovska Mitrovica, which is in the northern part of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic, and for the effort you have made to be as economical as possible in your use of the time, and we expect the same from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- finish today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We won't be able to finish today, and the witness will have to come back on Monday. Maybe the Chamber is about to take a break, I have no idea, but may I make this preparatory remark: Of course I not only aim for two thirds, I aim for much better than two-thirds, because of the reality that time on administration is out of my control. It comes out of the two-thirds. With a witness like this, particularly when he's been allowed - I make no complaint - to give the most general evidence on paragraphs in the indictment, it's not possible for me to cross-examine him fully and I shan't attempt to do so. I shall choose a sufficient number of topics I think will be helpful to the Chamber. Again by way of observations that may explain a little the shortening of what would be otherwise a full examination of this witness, the issue of the poisoning, I may ask a question about it. It was never raised by the Prosecution. It was raised in cross-examination of an early witness by the accused, and I subsequently asked one question, I think, of one witness. It doesn't seem to me to be a material issue and I shall almost certainly not raise it. As to the position of the doctors, it was in paragraph 67, or is it 87, of the indictment as background material. No evidence, as far as I can see, was led that was specifically related to discriminatory acts against doctors, simply for want of time. The accused chose not to engage himself in the process of analysis that came at the end of the Prosecution's case and has opened the issue up -- when he could have dealt with that as a matter if he wanted to -- and has opened the issue up. I will, in the circumstances and in light of what's been said, deal with that to some degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree with you about the doctors and that there is no allegation against doctors for discrimination. I'm not so sure I agree with you about your evaluation of the evidence relating to poison. It may be that the accused is saying that this particular behaviour was representative of how the Albanians behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly he is. He's raised it. It's not one of our allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before we move on, can we make 5.18, tab 15, tab 16, and tab 17 exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, please start, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The break is at quarter past.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quarter past. I completely lost track of time. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, a little bit more about yourself, please, if you'd be so good. You now, of course, only work in the Belgrade centred hospital in north Mitrovica; yes?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. That's not correct. I work in the clinical hospital centre of Pristina, which was temporary -- temporarily relegated to the northern part of Kosovska Mitrovica. It is not a Belgrade centred hospital, it is a Pristina hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Should you -- should you be known to the doctors in the Pristina hospital at the moment?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very probably. Maybe not all of them know me, but those that I have worked with know me. You mean Albanian doctors?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they know me. I can't imagine they forgot me so quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Dr. Andric, we had in advance of your giving evidence not very much information. I'll just explain: We were told as to you that you would give evidence about persecution of Albanians and their expulsion, about Yugoslav and Serb efforts to prevent propaganda motivated moving out, circumstances preceding the conflict, personal knowledge of facts, personal knowledge of activities of the parties, personal knowledge of the military, the police, and other armed activities. And we were also told you were a member of the provisional Executive Council, but that's all we got, you see. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I was a member of the provisional Executive Council, that is, the provisional government, as I mentioned in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we got this little file of exhibits just over a week, I think it was, wasn't it? About a week ago. And we had to work out what you were going to tell us by way of evidence. Let's just explore the provisional Executive Council a little bit more, and if time allows, a great deal more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused seems to be speaking to the witness, either asking him to answer a question or volunteering an answer. Perhaps he would be restrained from doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Mr. Robinson, I was addressing the liaison officer because I don't have the date in front of me. I was going to challenge the assertion that this file was given to Mr. Nice a week ago. This binder with various tabs was disclosed much more than a week ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Received on the 17th of February. What's the date today? Just over a week ago. A week ago. I was right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Andric, the history and summary of the temporary Executive Council is this: That following the change in Kosovo's constitutional position at the end of the 1980s, you will see what you said about it if necessary, there were no elections for many years, were there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There were no elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kosovo was simply administered directly by people from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there were no elections or, rather, there were elections, but one side, although able to participate in the elections, chose not to. It had that democratic right to take part in the elections, but they did not exercise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The elections actually happened and people were voted into office for governmental bodies, or were there no elections?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elections were held when the multi-party system was introduced in Serbia. However, Albanians before and during that period ignored the elections and did not turn up, did not turn out. Everybody else apart from the Albanians took part in the elections and voted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1998, the decision was made, and it ultimately was this accused's decision, was it not, to create this temporary Executive Council which was formally established by the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right, Mr. Nice. The provisional Executive Council was established at the second extraordinary session of the republic Assembly on the 28th of September, 1998, at the proposal of the government of Serbia, not the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having been established, presided over by Mr. Andjelkovic with you as a member, it had a range of functions, and you had a range of functions. As well as humanitarian functions, you were involved in the provincial civil protection staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of three different staffs in Kosovo, and I was a chairman or a president of one of the staffs. That was the staff for humanitarian affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as to the provincial civil protection staff, that was a staff that, amongst other things, had some authority over Civil Defence, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. But I believe that we never actually dealt with that problem within the staff. It was formally within our purview, but we never actually dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because that would have given you some authority over people exercising military or quasi-military functions, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as far as the provincial staff of Civil Defence, I can tell you that we never discussed any military units, nor did the staff have anything to do with it. That was the job of the military department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military department of the what, temporary Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no military department in the provincial -- in the provisional provincial council. We did not have such an organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your term. Which military department were you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the military department which was part of the army that recruited conscripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army and military department seem rather different terms maybe. Who was the representative of the army in Kosovo during your period of time as member of the provisional Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representative of the army in the provincial council, in the provisional provincial council? I don't know that such a job existed. The provisional provincial council dealt only with civilian issues of everyday life. We had no influence whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who dealt with military matters in Kosovo during your period on the council? Who was the general in charge?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, if I'm not mistaken, there was the Pristina Corps at the time, and the commander of that corps, if I'm not mistaken again, was General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Pavkovic, he was one of the members of another body called the Joint Command, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Joint Command you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Despite being in Kosovo throughout the bombing campaign to which the Yugoslav army had to respond, are you telling us that you weren't aware of the body that commanded the army? Perhaps I've got the name wrong.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you from my general knowledge who could have been in command of the army. I suppose the commander of the army of Yugoslavia. I'm not an expert in military matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a leading politician of the body that was now the public face of the administration of government in Kosovo. Kosovo faces NATO, and the army has much to do. Can you really not help us, Mr. Andric, with how it was, which was the body, which was the staff that ran the army? Can you really not help us?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I thank you for having such a high opinion of me as a politician. I'm afraid I am falling short of it. In any case, I can tell you quite honestly that I don't know who could have been in charge of the army if it wasn't the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. As for the provisional provincial council, I can assure you that we never ever discussed any military matters unless you mean the staff for the coordination of activities between civilian authorities and the Ministry of the Interior. That was my only contact with military personnel during the war. If that's what you mean, this coordination body, then that coordination body existed and it was active every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What military representation was there on that body?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that coordination staff there were two colonels; Colonel Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Stefanovic, Milomir Stefanovic, and Colonel Petkovic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What building was your council housed in?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our council was housed in the building of the provincial Executive Council on the high street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the high street. Did any other body inhabit that same building?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the building of the provisional provincial council. At that time, one wing of the building held two or three sections of the Ministry of Interior, but that was in the period when Albanians refused to take part in the official life of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Council probably later. Shall we look together, please, at some of your exhibits. Will you open the file at tab 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian interpretation, what Mr. Nice is saying is interpreted with the word "veca," and that word has many meanings, so the witness may be confused. If what they mean is provincial council, that is provincial government, it has to be clearly said, because "veca" has many different meanings. It means deliberation, it means review, it means board, it means what -- many things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for the clarification, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 1 is an example of the material that came to us one week ago and that we have to deal with or, alternatively, not to deal with. You're a scientific man. This is a piece of paper that tells us what? First of all, who prepared it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the services of the provincial secretariat for health care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They're not identified as the preparers on the document that I have. Does it tell us to which original material they turned for this analysis?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The documents come without any annex of original material for me to check, and you have not checked the figures yourself, have you, against original material? Have you?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have no reason not to believe my own technical services. If I disbelieved them, then I would have to check every document they make against original sources and that would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... important in all careful deliberations, whether scientific or forensic, and you will understand that I'm in no position to accept or reject the material you present on a single piece of paper with no supporting documentation or even identification of what the supporting documentation is. Shall we look at tab 2? Again a piece of paper prepared by staff of yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't check the figures yourself, no annex for me, no identification of the material that was relied on. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I trust my staff, and what you are saying is absolutely impossible. If we were to proceed the way you suggest, then it would be impossible for us to work at all. These figures were derived from the documents available in the health care organisations of Kosovo and Metohija, and they represent reality. They are absolutely accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to tab 3, please. Perhaps if Ms. Dicklich would help, or somebody, we could just lay a copy of this on the overhead projector for those viewing proceedings. This is a document originally headed "List by Departments of Teachers and Assistants of Medical Facilities [sic] in Pristina of Albanian Nationalities who Remained on Posts in Pristina City Hospital After," and it originally read 1999, but apparently that's an error and it should read 1991.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an error after interpretation -- of the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who prepared this list?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list was drafted by heads of chairs, professors, my colleagues, together with me, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can't see who these professors and heads of chairs are, but we can see quite a lot of names. Do we see on this list of names the people who prepared the lists or are they not on the document?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are some other people who prepared the lists?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what it says is these are the people who remained in Pristina city hospital, and we now know that the concern is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says medical faculty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are people who continued to work in the clinics and the institutions of the medical school of the Pristina University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the significance of this so I can understand your evidence? What's important about this, do you say?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The importance of this document, Mr. Nice, is that it shows that those who wanted to and who performed their work properly were able to continue working in the clinics and institutions of the medical school in Pristina. No pressure was put on them unless it was pressure by other Albanians who wanted them to leave their jobs there and go to work in parallel Albanian institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course here we've got real names, haven't we, of real professionals. And although sometimes they're marked as assistants, just to deal with this, the assistants are themselves qualified doctors. Is that right, first of all, assistants are qualified doctors?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are medical doctors. All of them are medical doctors. They only have different degrees, titles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In preparing this evidence to help this accused, knowing that you were going to name these people and for inferences to be drawn from them, did you contact them?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to. I had no way of contacting them. Because, Mr. Nice, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, I can only reach up to north Mitrovica. Further than that, I cannot set foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write them?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know where these people are any more. I lost all touch with them five years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... none of them remember you, but if there was a serious point -- well, let me just cut to the point. Given that we were provided with these names a week ago, you couldn't complain, could you, if as many of them as possible were contacted to see what they had to say about what you suggested. You couldn't complain about that, could you?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course until yesterday morning, our understanding, because we had this little tiny summary about your evidence and just these documents, was that the significance of this list was that it was about doctors who remained in post after 1999, which is of course a significant date. And if you cast your eye down, under the ophthalmology section, to the second name, number 2, it's a woman's name, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time she was seen two days ago, the Prosecution was justified in thinking that this was all about what happened to her in the latter part of this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's leave, we'll play the beginning, in any event, of a video. And, Your Honour, we have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just say something, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness said loud and clear that this indication of 1999 is a typographical error. It should read 1991. He corrected that mistake as soon as we opened this document. So it is pointless to prove now that it is not actually 1999. He said it himself yesterday. And the point here is that these are people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that this is what Mr. Nice wants to do. Let us proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honours will understand, the period 1999 is all part of the period post-1991. When we first saw this woman, or when she was first seen, all we knew was that of interest was the 1999 period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's just about time for the break, so we can take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. Can we distribute the transcript. Your Honour, this was an interview conducted in English and Albanian. For that reason it would take a long time to play in full. In the short time available since it was transmitted here, we've selected certain passages to play in full, and they have been shadowed or shaded in the text, and then with your leave, I'll go through what follows because I can deal with it more quickly, and then we'll come to the next part to play. So with Ms. Dicklich's assistance, we'll turn to the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just deal with this as a matter of law first of all because it's a novel proposition that's being introduced into the trial. What I understand is proposed by the Prosecution is that an interview of the lady named as Meshqyre Capuni-Brestovci, which was taken a few days ago, on the 22nd of February, be played as a tool of cross-examination. It's a way of introducing evidence through that witness in the form of a video recording which this witness will be asked, or I hope, or to comment upon. Traditionally cross-examination is -- takes place in the form of questions by the advocate who puts his case and then may call evidence in rebuttal or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a video recording that is reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And I think what's proposed to be played is that this witness's -- well, she's not a witness. This person's interview, which hasn't been a part of the evidence in any shape or form, is then played and then this witness, who is the witness, be asked to comment on what is played. It's no different from having a statement, say, from the witness, that be put before the witness and them asked to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what do you hope to achieve by this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I remain astonished by my learned friend Mr. Kay's traditional approach to evidential problems that should not be confined to national approaches. And before I answer Your Honour's point, we must have in mind that this last -- this witness has been permitted to bring in endless statements by other people, hearsay of the most general kind: "I know that nobody was kicked out by anybody except the KLA" or whatever it can be summarised as. Statements in video form from television reporters, interviews with individuals. And what I'm proposing to do on a topic that has been raised by this accused, not by us, with, as I have revealed, minimum notice, is to put a case relating to one of the very people upon whose actions he relies. Now, yes, I can simply stand here and read out the contents of her statement and say that's the truth, isn't it? But which is going to be more helpful for the Tribunal, for me to do that or for the Tribunal to see the witness speaking? Let me say straight away, after this I do have another statement, at the moment in written form, for reasons entirely outside my control and a result of the conduct of the Defence which I shall also be seeking to lay before you, and I'll explain that when the time comes. But really, to say that these statements are not valuable or shouldn't be admitted would be to be applying entirely different standards for the Prosecution than for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course you cannot enlarge your case, and I'm concerned as to whether this is what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can put it if you're seeking to test the credibility of the witness or to contradict the witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in answer to the first point, I'm not actually sure about that. If the defendant or the accused chooses to raise another issue which could fall -- I'm mean, I'm not sure that it falls to anything except background at the moment, but if he raises an issue that could form part of the case and he chooses to do so, and Defence evidence can always be part of a Prosecution case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course. You can seek to contradict anything that he raises or to test the credibility of the witness on any point that he raises, but apart from that, you can't enlarge your case. But I certainly am of the view that you are entitled to put to the witness something which serves to contradict the evidence of the accused's witness or to test his credibility. And what is it that you're seeking to do here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the witness what is the significance about the evidence he's given about these people whose names he listed as being present since 1991 and thus, of course, through 1999, and he gave his answer. We now need to know what the position of those witnesses would be. He didn't make any efforts to contact them. This is an inquiry into the truth, and for the Chamber to be -- with proof. But for the Chamber to be invited to draw extraordinarily wide inferences by the generalised evidence of this witness whose partiality is something to which I will turn and thus whose credibility is in issue would be quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm concerned about some consistency in our practice. I remember that we didn't allow the accused to put some comments of a third party on the witness's evidence of previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't immediately recall what Your Honour has in mind, but this is not -- I remember what Your Honour has in mind. This is witnesses commenting on evidence. Yes, we had a couple of occasions of that and Judge May said call the witness. Well, that was -- it's the same point we've raised before. It is one thing for the Prosecution case where a Defence case is certain. It is entirely different for a Defence case when the prospects of a rebuttal case are uncertain. It's entirely different for an issue that's been raised by this accused afresh and without notice. I've made complaints before, and I'm going to repeat them, about the complete inadequacy for the forensic process of these 65 ter summaries with which I am supposed to work, and I have to make it quite plain that it is becoming increasingly difficult for the Prosecution to serve this Chamber properly when it is presented with a mass of material at short notice with which we have to deal in a confined period of time. Now, here we have the clearest possible example, and let me explain exactly what this witness says on her tape so there can be no doubt about it for the purposes of the record. She says that on the 24th of March, 1999, the situation was tense. People were afraid. When she tried to go to work in a neighbourhood that's a bit -- she lives a bit further away, she heard a bullet. She wasn't conscious of what was happening. She was advised to go home and did so. She notified the director of the hospital what the problem was, and he said, "I will give you -- he said, "I'll give you a document" which would assist her. She then used that document, and on the 31st of March, when she came back again after a time away, her neighbourhood was completely surrounded by concentrations of police forces who told us that -- told them that they had to leave their homes. So those were the particular circumstances of the 24th of March. If you go down to clip 2, she didn't want -- she went back to her sister's she didn't want to make the circumstances even worse and decided to go to the Macedonian border, were directed towards Tetovo and towards Globocica and went in that direction. They spent seven days at the border which was opened sometimes and was being closed again in conditions that were cruel. If you turn over to the third clip, she went back home. She stayed at home for ten days, not daring to go out because of concentrations of troops in the area, looked out of the windows and eventually decided to go out on her own, believing that the document she had with her would save her - that's the document from the hospital director. She went to her sister's, she then went to the hospital to get her salary, and was then refused to work at the hospital. So that for circumstances entirely outside her control and despite even having the advantage of some laissez-passer by the director of the hospital, she was denied the opportunity to work, whether under some technical failure to turn up for a week or otherwise. Clip 4: She was asked a question were you aware or are subsequently aware of colleagues that practised, any Albanian colleagues that practised at Pristina hospital during this period of time you covered, and she said I didn't know anything. We'd also one week off at the time so I didn't know and I had no way of knowing. But afterwards I found out at the border that people had gone to Skopje and Macedonia. And actually there were two of my colleagues who were there with me at the border. We met them. We didn't go there. We met at the border. And finally she said, clip 5 - there's a lot of other stuff in between - Did you go back to work at the hospital? I was immediately after the NATO forces entered and I don't remember the date. Now, with Your Honours' leave, I'm going to distribute another document because in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say that goes to? What issue raised by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The history --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. My mike wasn't on. I'm asking you what issue does that go to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Firstly, this was premised on the document that hadn't been corrected two days before, and so we thought that the accused was interested in presenting evidence of what was the reality for Albanian doctors staying on in March 1999, and the reality for this Albanian doctor, the only one that was possible to identify out of the list he's relied upon, is that despite all efforts and because of what was happening to her and in the surrounding area, she couldn't get back to work and was forbidden from working by the director of that hospital. So that's extremely important. But, Your Honour, what happened was the -- and perhaps we can distribute the Pallaska statement, please. But what happened was when the correction was made to tab whatever it is, 3, and 1999 was converted to 1991, I gave instructions and we attempted to return to the same woman to ask the questions about the period of 1991 on. It wasn't possible to find her again in the short period of time because then it was hoped that this evidence might finish today, but it was possible to find another doctor who had -- not one of the ones on the list. It doesn't matter. A doctor who had been present since 1991 and had carried on working. So with that doctor and with this doctor we have some account for a topic raised by this accused which he need never have raised, he's chosen to do so, dealing with what happened to this doctor in the period 1991 onwards. Your Honours, so this statement again, and I repeat, having no detail -- let me just pause for a minute because it's time I made this point again for the sake of the record and so that the Prosecution's position can be well understood: The accused, when he came to deal with witnesses not only had been served witness statements in great detail months in advance, notified usually weeks in advance that witnesses were coming, but he was provided with summaries of the precise evidence the witness was going to give and was also provided, as on this occasion we were a week ago, with the precise exhibits that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't wish to hear you any more on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has ruled on it. In my view the relationship between the Prosecutor and the accused is not a symmetrical one, it's asymmetrical. The Prosecutor has burdens and duties which the accused does not have. The accused has rights which the Prosecutor does not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases, but that imposes on me the duty to do everything I can to meet things that arise by way of therefore justifiable surprise. This doctor then, and we can see it on page 2 of the document, says he was practising in the hospital in 1989 and was one of the doctors that was not removed from his post. He was unaware of any Albanian doctors that left service at Pristina from 1989 onwards with the specific intention of setting up in private practice. He deals with the particular circumstances of his father who did leave and set up private practice. He says, "I am unaware of any doctors that left service at Pristina hospital after 1989 through to 1998 without being dismissed by the hospital." Next paragraph, or next heading he says this, and this is specifically contrary to something that this witness has dealt with and I will be asking him about it. He sets out the reasons for doctors being dismissed from service, perhaps because they completed medical forms in the Albanian language, not in Serbian and other reasons are given. Next paragraph. He deals with the sanctions that would be imposed on Albanian doctors speaking to Albanian patients other than in the Serbian language. He then explains the history of doctors being dismissed in late 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, thank you. I just want to ask Mr. Kay, why shouldn't the Prosecutor in cross-examination be entitled to put to a witness for the Defence a document which, on the basis of answers that he might receive from the witness, could serve to contradict the evidence of that witness or to throw some doubt on his credibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's cross-examination. These are cross-examination materials for the Prosecutor. They're not evidence. Let's start, first of all, with the video. A videotape of this woman is played. The accused doesn't have an opportunity to cross-examine the witness in the videotape, so you hear her account. He's asked questions, "Well, what do you think of that? You heard her say there that." She is being used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that all go to weight, the weight that is attached?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It doesn't go to weight. His evidence is the important issue here. That video clip is being used as a means of putting a witness into the Defence case, a very familiar tactic that we've had continuously throughout the Defence and that the accused was restrained from doing. He was told, "Your time will come when you can call evidence." Mr. Nice's case will have another section to it in a rebuttal case. He says, "I don't know whether I'll have a rebuttal case." That plainly is unrealistic, and I believe a few days ago Your Honour said to him, what are you saying you're not going to get a chance of a rebuttal case? If this is being done as a means of -- because he's not going to get a rebuttal case, we don't accept that at all. What is being done through the video is a way of putting evidence into the Court that he, the accused, is unable to deal with by the means of the cross-examination. All counsel -- and it's a difficult job being an advocate, and I'll echo the words there of my learned friend to me once -- it's a difficult job being counsel. You have to sometimes ask questions, you have to deal with what you have, and then you deal with it in a proper, admissible form whereby the evidence can be properly tested. Otherwise, Your Honours are being subjected to materials in a technological form that are being used to advance the Prosecution case in a way that it becomes their case. What they should be doing is challenging through the advocate, through putting questions, this particular witness's account, and then if they disagree with this witness's account, calling evidence to rebut it. And that is a procedure recognised within the Rules. The witness statement, as he has cross-examined other witnesses before, he will have had materials. He puts to this witness from the materials he has to hand the questions he seeks to ask to test the evidence. The statement may come in in his rebuttal case as evidence, through Rule 92 bis, or it may be through calling the witness live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The fact that he can adduce it in rebuttal doesn't necessarily mean that he can't adduce it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm not saying that. What I'm saying is he should put questions. Mr. Milosevic was told to put questions and not make statements. This is no different from Mr. Nice making a statement on the strength of his case. It's no different from that, Your Honour. It's exactly what is going on in a much more subtle form and through the video using a technological aid, but it's actually making a statement of his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. case during the questioning of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not a statement of his case. He's using it to contradict the case that Mr. Milosevic is putting forward, that all Albanian doctors were able to work without any kind of molestation. Why shouldn't he be able to contradict that evidence in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He is by asking the questions. That is the function of it. And the materials he may produce in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Only in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He is using -- he is using it as his case rather than contradiction. He's already said that to you. He has given the reasoning behind it, saying he has evidence here relating to a different state of affairs in 1999. He wishes, in the interests of, as he sees it, putting the truth before the Court, to make sure the Court has that material now. So it's not a process of contradiction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't accept that characterisation by Mr. Nice. I think it is essentially evidence which contradicts may test the credibility, and if that has the incidental effect of becoming part of the Prosecution case, that's an incidental effect. But don't you deprive cross-examination of its essential sting if you prevent the cross-examiner from putting a document to a witness which may serve to contradict what he says? Isn't that the whole purpose of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We could break it down further. In these proceedings he could put a document. It's then what happens to the document. If he plays the video, he's just playing the content from the witness and that witness's statement. He's not doing the job of challenging the witness. He's doing it through the statements being made in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the witness can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is evidence that is being introduced by the Prosecution in a form that is for the truth of the statement rather than to challenge this witness. The accused is unable himself to cross-examine the person who is being used in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not opposing to putting the material to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you are opposing is playing the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I could see that this could come to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can see it becoming a coach and horses and I have had experience in the trial how one ruling then enables the Prosecution to open up a particular advance front and through it produce a great deal of materials, and I suspect that is behind this here, that once it is done, it then becomes the commonplace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I make -- can I reply, just two or three points, because it's absolutely essential that the fallacy and limitation of that last argument is laid bare. My learned friend, throughout the evidence of this witness, kept reminding the Chamber to admit tabs 5.2, tab 5.3, tab 5.4. As a friend of the Court, he should have been, on his latest argument, saying you can't admit these because these are actually being adduced for the truth of their content. He should have been saying Mr. Nice can't cross-examine this man in the leather hat. It so happens, that as we go through the tabs we'll find that eventually there comes a time when one of these witnesses was named, and you can be quite sure I've been and I've made every effort to speak to the named witnesses, because that was an appropriate course, but what he's arguing is completely inconsistent with the position he's taken. And I must respectfully remind the Chamber that there have been, from the Defence side, innumerable documents, newspaper articles and all sorts of things admitted in on various bases but plainly the ultimate purpose of which is to have the truth of their content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say of his remark that in the Prosecution case Mr. Milosevic was told time and again -- was prevented time and again from introducing evidence of that kind and told that he should wait his turn?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've already dealt with that point on several occasions, now and in the past, and of course if the Chamber decides that the position has to be varied or adjusted because of the state of the trial we're in, so be it, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's better to be correct than consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour could put it like that, yes. But the suggestion also that somehow we have to go through the extraordinarily artificial exercise of my converting into reported speech what is available to you in a better form is nonsense. We're going to come to an example, for example, with one or two of the people that this witness has spoken of, if we get the time, as having said things favourable, or by implication favourable. Now, those people have made contradictory statements in the public format; newspapers, press reports, whatever else it is. Am I entitled to put those statements or do I have to stand here, as Mr. Kay would say, and say, Isn't it right in relation to international personality Mr. X that the position was this not that? No. You say this is what Mr. X said. What's your comment on that? That's the way we've been proceeding throughout. And although the accused may have been subject to some limitations on putting in witness statements when they weren't related to evidence before the Chamber, that's different, you may think, from the present position where the evidence is here and we've got another statement by the same person to a contrary effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you wanted to say something? I was asking if you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. Robinson. I did hear you. I was waiting for the interpretation to finish, because the interpretation was still coming through my headphones. I only wish to draw your attention to one single reason why this transcript and video clip that Mr. Nice has now provided cannot be compared to tab 5 in which I provided video clips to accompany the examination of this witness. There is a difference here. In those clips, you were able to see the witness. The witness was present at those events. Those statements were made in his presence together with other members of the provincial -- provisional provincial Executive Council; Ibrahimi, Jashari, and the third one. They were there and they could hear what those people were saying. They were talking to them. So this is a completely different situation from a situation in which a video clip of something a doctor said on the 24th of March, 1999, is portrayed, and this allegedly refers to the document provided by this witness. However, it is very clearly stated that this document provided by the witness relates to 1991 and not 1999. These are two completely different things. Tab 5 does not contain hearsay evidence. This is evidence at which the witness was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, coming from the jurisdiction from which you do, I think you would appreciate that point. The presence of the witness in the interviews does make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't understand the point of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was saying that the essential difference between his videos and the one that you're now seeking to present is that in his videos, the witness was ever present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. The videos -- and this is another serious problem that we're going to have to encounter, as you'll see from the third document that I'm going to present to you at a later stage unless something happens which I'll turn to in a second. They're not present in the sense of present when they're being expelled from their houses. They're not present when the bombs are dropping. They're present, being interviewed, after the event by reporters. The only difference here is that they're being interviewed after the event by an investigator. There is no difference of class at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's saying that the witness himself was present --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness himself, so questions could be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was only present at some, very few. And at the moment we've got no evidence of his being the interlocutor or the interviewer of any of the people who give their particular accounts. He's given a generalised account. If we go through these clips and look at the various individuals, they're being spoken to by journalists, not by him, and there's no evidence that he was present save on a limited number of occasions. And can I explain why I said I'll reach the third position or the third piece of material that I want to lay before you of this general kind soon, unless something happens. The thing that would happen is this: If there is to be any question of excision of material of this kind, my next application will be to remove all of the hearsay evidence from this witness's evidence, which would take out all the tabs, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it were -- if it were agreed to by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But that would be my application, because there are simply different standards being applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the essential difficulty that we have here, and it's a jurisprudential one, is the mixing of the civil law flexible system with more strict conditions of admissibility from the common law system, and until we resolve that we're always going to face this issue. 89(C) sends us down the civil law flexible route. But Mr. Kay makes points which, in my view, are more drawn from the common law system, objecting to admissibility. But I'm going now to consult my colleague on this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The ruling is that you can put the statements but not the videos, and the admission of the statements will depend on the answers given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have before the witness on the overhead projector, please, the statement of Meshqyre Capuni-Brestovci. Put it on the overhead projector and I'm going to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has the statement before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whose statement is it, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statement is the statement of Meshqyre Capuni, and it is, unfortunately, in English in light of the brevity of time, and I'm going to read passages of it to this witness and ask him whether he accepts that this can be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, this woman whose name you relied on said, amongst other things, the following: That on the 24th of March of 1999, all her colleagues were working. She's in the hospital. The situation was tense, and everyone was afraid after finishing their normal working hours so they went home so that they could go back to work the next day. Any reason to doubt that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness provided under tab 3 the list of doctors who remained working after 1991, and I see that under number 2, we have the name of this person, and next to her name it says that she was a lecturer. The witness explained that the list was drawn by the chairs of departments and that this person remained working up to 1991. So what would the statement of this woman about what happened in 1999 have to do with the evidence given by this witness? In tab 3, the witness claims and provided a list of the doctors who worked after 1991. Now, what Mr. Nice is saying now, does it contradict in any way what this witness told us earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, look at page 2 under "JS". It says, "I could ask you to take it from there in your own words. Would you just explain your experiences from the 24th of March, 1999." And Mr. Milosevic is asking how that will help us in relation to the experiences in 1991 relating to her work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It helps because this witness has given a general account of the freedom of Albanian doctors to work at all periods of time starting in 1991 and onwards. Your Honour, in fact before we come to that, and I'm going to interrupt the flow of my questions because it occurs to me in light of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Court's ruling that I must now apply that all the videotape evidence under tabs 5 and onwards, save for the limited passages that actually show this witness, that they all be now ruled as inadmissible for the reasons advanced by Mr. Kay in his argument if it is for those reasons that the Chamber is denying me the opportunity to play this video. If we're going to achieve consistency, then now is the time to start. And if there is to be a general rule that a videotape of what somebody says in answer to interview questions is inadmissible even though it's on a relevant topic, then it's my duty to try to achieve consistency now, which I do. I haven't, of course, gone through, I'm afraid, all of the tabs with a view to checking exactly which ones would remain admissible even if my argument succeeds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to deal with that now. I note the application you have made. Just move on with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Well, then, my -- and obviously this evidence will be being dealt with, as it were, subject to the resolution of that application. The --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, perhaps I failed to understand, but where does the difference lie between reading the transcript of a videotape and playing a videotape? Why would you allow the transcript to be read and not allow the videotape? Let us play the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is his case. I've said this before: If he wants it played, let's play it. It will be much quicker.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is not my case. However, Mr. Nice insists upon the tape being played, and he takes it as a reason for challenging other exhibits. I don't mind him playing any tape he wants to play. However, that's his motion, not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The tape can be played on the basis that there is no objection from the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. If we can just play the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, for the record, I want to be sure that it is recorded that this conversation was conducted on the 22nd of February, 2005, this interview. This is stated on the transcript. I'm not sure whether it is obvious on the tape as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Play the first part of it, then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The situation was tense. And after finishing the working hours we went home so we could go back to work the next day. The next day, when I tried to go to work, I lived in neighbourhood that is a bit further away, in Velania, and I was walking on the road from my house to go to work and I heard a bullet pass over my head. And I was -- I wasn't even conscious of what was happening but a neighbour told me to -- to move away from that place. And I went home, and after some time had passed, around midday I tried to go to work again. It was Friday. And I -- I notified the director, of the hospital, that is, of what the problem was and he said I'll give you document, and he said that he would give -- he would give me a document which would allow me to walk through the city and to go to work and because a colleague of mine had already asked for a document. And I -- on Saturday or Sunday, a friend of mine called me and she said that the director had given permission for us to miss the following week, and so we didn't have to go and work. "Then the 31st -- then the 31st of March came when our neighbourhood was completely surrounded by large concentrations of police forces. And then they expelled us. They told us that we had to leave our homes in five minutes, within five minutes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, pausing there, Dr. Andric, page 80 of the yesterday's transcript, you were the provisional or you were the secretary of health. Any reason to doubt a word of what you've just heard?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, Mr. Nice, I have to tell you that when you previously addressed His Honour Robinson, you said that I had said that this was a document showing Albanian professors and doctors working in clinics between 1991 and 1999. I never said that, and that is not true. This document reflects the doctors, professors, and associates of the medical school who remained working in 1991 in various clinics and institutes. Now, whether they remained working until 1999 or 1992 is not something that I ever went into, nor is it relevant for this document. The purpose of this document was to show that all those who wanted to stay --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. We've gone through the history of the error in the document that was presented on your behalf, and it was the error of that document that led to the bifurcated interviewing of two different doctors which we're going to examine. My question to you is quite simple and it arises as relevant because as provisional secretary of health, as you've told us on page 80 of the transcript, you made it clear that - and I quote - you issued an order addressed to the heads of all health institutions in Kosovo and Metohija to ensure that health professionals continued in their work. And we're going so see what happened to this health professional. I want to break it down. In the first part that you've heard, is there any reason to doubt a word of what she says?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have equal reasons to doubt as to believe, because I know what the official position was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This woman is a doctor. Doesn't make her into a different category. She's been prepared to make a statement. You tell us, please, is there any reason to doubt what you've seen? Do you actually have any material, any evidence? You've given the most general sweeping statements today. Any hard reason to doubt what you've heard?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you, Mr. Nice, why there could be reasons to doubt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, my microphone was not turned on, so -- rather, the witness's microphone was not turned on so I didn't hear his entire answer. His microphone was not turned on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that it is on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber would be good enough to look at the text just before clip 2, you will see that in the statement the witness explains how at her sister's address she was told -- where they pretended to be Turks, she was told by visiting soldiers that if there were any Albanians, they shouldn't make the mistake of staying there.
